cards.simple: HOW MUCH to order each time.
cards.hook: EOQ has Q for Quantity. Quantity = how much.
cards.example: Bob always orders 447 buns. Fewer and he pays order fees constantly. More and he pays to store a mountain of buns. 447 is the sweet spot.
cards.answer: The order size that keeps the combined cost of placing orders and storing stock as low as possible.
traps: The stock level that signals it's time to place the next order.
The order size that gets the lowest price per unit from the supplier.
The order size that keeps storage costs as low as possible, ignoring ordering costs.
cards.confuse: ROP is WHEN to order. EOQ is HOW MUCH.

cards.simple: WHEN to order. The stock level that says "order now."
cards.hook: It's the low-fuel light on your gas gauge.
cards.example: Bob uses 20 lb of beef a day, delivery takes 5 days, plus 30 lb backup: 20×5 + 30 = 130. When beef hits 130 lb, he calls.
cards.answer: The inventory level that tells you to place the next order.
traps: The amount you should order each time you restock.
The inventory level where you've completely run out.
The number of days it takes a delivery to arrive.
cards.confuse: EOQ is how much. ROP is when.
cards.formula: ROP = (Daily demand × Lead time) + Safety stock

cards.full: uses COGS = Cost of Goods Sold
cards.simple: HOW FAST stuff sells and gets restocked in a year.
cards.hook: How many times a year the fridge goes empty → full.
cards.example: Bob's COGS is $120,000 and his average inventory is $20,000. 120,000 ÷ 20,000 = 6 turns a year.
cards.answer: How many times a year the average inventory gets sold through and replaced.
traps: Average inventory divided by cost of goods sold.
How many times a year you place an order with suppliers.
How many days it takes for one order to sell out.
cards.confuse: COGS goes on top, average inventory on the bottom.

cards.simple: Stuff sells fast. Profit comes in and storage costs drop.
cards.hook: A bakery that sells out every day. Nothing goes stale.
cards.example: Bob's beef is gone within days of arriving. Kahoot: why it matters = profit realized + lower holding costs.
cards.answer: Product moves quickly, so money comes back fast and less is spent storing it.
traps: Product moves quickly, so holding costs go up because you reorder more often.
Product moves slowly, so there's always plenty on hand.
Product moves quickly, which guarantees you'll never run out.
cards.confuse: Too high can mean running out (stockouts).

cards.simple: Stuff sits around. Cash is stuck and it can spoil.
cards.example: Bob buys 6 months of beef but barely sells burgers. It sits in the freezer eating his money.
cards.answer: Product moves slowly, tying up cash and raising storage costs.
traps: Product moves slowly, which lowers holding costs because you order less.
Product moves quickly, but each sale earns very little.
Product moves slowly because demand is perfectly predictable.

cards.simple: An INSIDE request: "Can I buy this?"
cards.hook: Like asking your parents before you buy something.
cards.example: The chef asks Bob: "Can we order 100 lb of beef?"
cards.answer: An internal form an employee uses to ask permission to buy something.
traps: The official order sent to a supplier listing items and prices.
An internal form a manager uses to approve a supplier's bill.
A request sent to suppliers asking for their prices.
cards.confuse: A requisition stays INSIDE. A PO goes OUTSIDE.

cards.simple: The boss says yes to the request.
cards.example: Linda reads the chef's request and says "Approved."
cards.answer: Someone with authority signs off on the request so the buying can move forward.
traps: The supplier agrees to fill the order.
An employee confirms the goods arrived.
The manager sends the official order to the supplier.
cards.confuse: Approval happens inside your company. Acceptance comes from the supplier.

cards.simple: The official order sent OUTSIDE to the supplier.
cards.example: Linda emails the supplier a PO: 100 lb beef, $4/lb, deliver Friday.
cards.answer: The formal document a buyer sends a supplier spelling out the items, amounts, prices and terms.
traps: An internal form asking a manager for permission to buy.
The bill a supplier sends after delivering the goods.
The supplier's reply agreeing to sell at the set price.
cards.confuse: Sending the PO isn't binding yet. It's binding when the supplier accepts.

cards.simple: The supplier says yes. NOW the PO is legally binding.
cards.hook: The handshake. No handshake, no deal.
cards.example: The supplier replies "Confirmed for Friday." Both sides are now locked in.
cards.answer: The supplier agrees to the PO's terms, which makes the deal legally binding.
traps: The buyer sends the PO, which makes the deal legally binding.
A manager approves the request, which makes the deal legally binding.
The goods get delivered, which is the first point the deal is binding.

cards.simple: Request → Approve → Order → Accept.
cards.example: The chef asks → Linda approves → Linda sends the PO → the supplier agrees.
cards.answer: Requisition, then approval, then purchase order, then supplier acceptance.
traps: Purchase order, then requisition, then approval, then supplier acceptance.
Requisition, then purchase order, then approval, then supplier acceptance.
Approval, then requisition, then purchase order, then supplier acceptance.
cards.question: What's the correct purchasing sequence?

cards.simple: Request for Information. "Tell me about yourselves."
cards.hook: I = Info. Like checking someone's profile before a first date.
cards.example: Bob asks 5 beef companies what they sell and where they deliver.
cards.answer: An early ask for general details about suppliers and what they're capable of.
traps: An ask for suppliers to explain how they'd solve your specific need.
An ask for suppliers' exact prices on specific items.
An internal ask for permission to contact suppliers.
cards.confuse: RFI = get to know them. RFP = their plan. RFQ = their price.

cards.simple: Request for Proposal. "Show me your plan."
cards.hook: P = Plan / Proposal. They pitch you a solution.
cards.example: Bob asks: "How would you keep my restaurant stocked with beef every week?"
cards.answer: An ask for suppliers to lay out how they'd meet your requirements.
traps: An ask for general background on what a supplier does.
An ask for exact prices on items you've already specified.
The formal order you send once you've picked a supplier.
cards.confuse: RFP is about their solution. RFQ is about the numbers.

cards.simple: Request for Quotation. "What's your price?" Detailed cost numbers.
cards.example: Bob asks for the exact price of 100 lb delivered weekly. Supplier: $4.10/lb.
cards.answer: An ask for exact pricing on goods you've already specified.
traps: An ask for suppliers to propose how they'd solve your problem.
An ask for general info on what suppliers can do.
The supplier's final bill for goods already delivered.
cards.confuse: Kahoot: the one with detailed cost numbers is the RFQ.

cards.simple: The usual order: get info, hear the plan, then talk price.
cards.hook: Meet them → hear the pitch → talk money.
cards.example: Bob learns who's out there, asks two of them for plans, then gets final price quotes.
cards.answer: Learn about suppliers, then see their solutions, then compare prices.
traps: Compare prices, then see solutions, then learn about suppliers.
Learn about suppliers, then compare prices, then see solutions.
See solutions, then learn about suppliers, then compare prices.
cards.question: What's the usual order of RFI, RFP and RFQ?

cards.simple: Everyday inventory for normal demand.
cards.example: The beef and buns Bob goes through on a normal Tuesday. Kahoot: this meets immediate customer demand.
cards.answer: Stock kept to cover regular, expected sales.
traps: Extra stock kept in case demand spikes or a delivery is late.
Stock that's currently on its way from the supplier.
Stock bought early because prices are expected to rise.
cards.confuse: Cycle = normal demand. Safety = surprises.

cards.simple: Backup stock in case of surprises.
cards.example: An extra 30 lb of beef for when a tour bus shows up or the truck is late.
cards.answer: Extra stock held as a cushion against surprise demand or late deliveries.
traps: Stock held to cover regular, expected daily sales.
Extra stock bought because prices are about to go up.
Stock that's in transit between the supplier and the store.
cards.confuse: Safety = random surprises. Strategic = a problem you see coming.

cards.simple: Inventory on the move, in transit.
cards.example: The beef riding on the delivery truck down the highway right now.
cards.answer: Goods that are currently moving between places in the supply chain.
traps: Goods sitting in a warehouse waiting to be sold.
Goods held as backup for unexpected demand.
Goods partway through being made.
cards.confuse: WIP is being MADE. Pipeline is being MOVED.

cards.simple: A stockpile for a future problem, like a shortage or a price jump.
cards.example: Bob hears oil prices will spike, so he buys 3 months of oil today.
cards.answer: Stock built up ahead of an expected shortage or price increase.
traps: Extra stock held for random, unpredictable demand spikes.
Stock kept to cover regular daily sales.
Stock built up only to qualify for bulk discounts.

cards.simple: Ingredients before anything gets made.
cards.example: Raw patties, cheese and buns in Bob's fridge.
cards.answer: Inputs that haven't gone into production yet.
traps: Items that have started production but aren't done.
Supplies that keep equipment running but never become part of the product.
Products that are complete and ready to sell.

cards.simple: Work-in-Process: started but not finished.
cards.example: A patty sizzling on the grill, with no bun on it yet.
cards.answer: Items that have entered production but aren't complete yet.
traps: Items moving in transit between locations.
Inputs that haven't entered production yet.
Finished items waiting to be shipped.
cards.confuse: Kahoot: WIP stands for Work-in-Process.

cards.simple: Done and ready to sell.
cards.example: A wrapped burger on the counter, waiting for pickup.
cards.answer: Completed products ready to be sold or shipped.
traps: Products partway through production.
Products that have sold but haven't been paid for yet.
Inputs waiting to go into production.

cards.simple: Maintenance, Repair & Operating supplies. Keeps things running and NEVER goes into the product.
cards.hook: You don't eat the grill cleaner.
cards.example: Spare grill parts, mops and light bulbs at Bob's.
cards.answer: Supplies that keep equipment and operations running but never become part of what's sold.
traps: Parts that get built into the final product during production.
Products partway through production.
Backup ingredients kept for unexpected demand.
cards.confuse: Kahoot: "MRO ends up in the final product" is FALSE.

cards.simple: Stuff that helps run the business but isn't the product.
cards.example: Dish soap at Bob's.
cards.answer: Items that support running the business or delivering a service, not the product itself.
traps: The main ingredients that become the finished product.
Items that are still in production.
Inventory being shipped out to customers.
cards.confuse: Kahoot: NOT a category of inventory for a product.

cards.simple: Total cost goes up and down with how busy you are.
cards.example: Ben's Diner uses more dish soap in peak season (that was the Kahoot).
cards.answer: A cost whose total rises and falls with business activity.
traps: A cost you can trace to one specific product.
A cost that stays the same no matter how busy you are.
A cost whose price per unit rises as you get busier.
cards.confuse: Variable vs fixed = does it change with activity? Direct vs indirect = can you trace it?

cards.simple: The same cost no matter how busy you are.
cards.example: Rent is $3,000 whether Bob sells 10 burgers or 1,000.
cards.answer: A cost whose total stays about the same even when activity goes up or down.
traps: A cost that can't be traced to any one product.
A cost whose total rises as you get busier.
A cost that can never change for any reason.

cards.simple: You can point at the exact product it went into.
cards.hook: It went directly into the burger.
cards.example: The patty inside burger #47.
cards.answer: A cost you can trace straight to a specific product.
traps: A cost whose total changes with activity.
A cost spread across the whole operation.
A cost paid in cash right away instead of on credit.
cards.confuse: Beef can be BOTH direct and variable.

cards.simple: Helps everything, but you can't pin it on one product.
cards.example: The kitchen's electricity bill.
cards.answer: A cost that supports the whole operation but can't easily be tied to one product.
traps: A cost that stays the same regardless of activity.
A cost traced straight to a specific product.
A cost that gets paid later instead of right away.

cards.simple: Have it when the customer wants it. The #1 reason to hold inventory.
cards.example: A customer orders a cheeseburger and Bob actually has cheese.
cards.answer: Keeping product on hand so it's there the moment a customer wants it.
traps: Keeping extra product to look bigger than competitors.
Keeping product on hand only during busy seasons.
Keeping product mainly to qualify for bulk discounts.

cards.simple: Stock up before a busy time you know is coming.
cards.example: Extra buns before the 4th of July weekend.
cards.answer: Building up stock before a busy period you can predict.
traps: Building up stock before an expected price increase.
Building up stock in case of random demand spikes.
Building up stock to cover the wait for the next delivery.
cards.confuse: Seasonal = predictable busy times. Safety = random surprises.

cards.simple: Buy in bulk to save money.
cards.example: Buns are cheaper per bun when Bob orders 1,000 at once.
cards.answer: Buying bigger amounts to get a lower cost per unit or place fewer orders.
traps: Buying smaller amounts more often to cut storage costs.
Buying from several suppliers to reduce risk.
Buying early because prices are about to rise.

cards.simple: Enough stock to last until the next delivery arrives.
cards.example: Delivery takes 5 days, so Bob keeps at least 5 days of beef.
cards.answer: Holding enough to keep selling while you wait for the next delivery.
traps: Holding extra in case demand is higher than normal.
Holding enough to qualify for volume discounts.
Holding stock that's currently in transit.

cards.term: NOT a Reason to Hold Inventory
cards.simple: Holding tons just to have more than competitors.
cards.hook: Bragging rights don't pay the bills.
cards.example: Bob buys double Jimmy Pesto's beef just to flex. Half of it spoils.
cards.answer: Keeping big piles of stock just to out-stock competitors.
traps: Keeping stock to cover the wait for deliveries.
Keeping stock to handle a predictable busy season.
Keeping stock to protect against supplier delays.
cards.question: Which is NOT a valid reason to hold inventory?

cards.simple: Radio waves read the tags. No need to aim a scanner.
cards.hook: R = Radio. Like E-ZPass reading your car as you drive by.
cards.example: Bob rolls a crate of tagged beef past a reader and every box gets counted.
cards.answer: Tags read by radio waves, so items don't need to be in the scanner's line of sight.
traps: Printed codes read by a laser that has to see the label.
Tags read by radio waves, but only one at a time with direct aim.
A camera system that photographs each item's label.
cards.confuse: Barcode needs to be SEEN. RFID doesn't.

cards.simple: The scanner has to SEE the barcode.
cards.example: Tina points the scanner right at the label on the box.
cards.answer: Printed codes read by an optical scanner that needs a clear view of the label.
traps: Tags read by radio waves without needing line of sight.
Printed codes that can be read through boxes and walls.
Tags that constantly broadcast their own location.

cards.simple: Basic, steady products. Predictable demand, low profit margin.
cards.example: Flour and napkins: people buy about the same amount all year.
cards.answer: Everyday products with steady demand, long life cycles and thin margins.
traps: New products with hard-to-predict demand and big margins.
Everyday products with steady demand and big margins.
Everyday products with short life cycles and unpredictable demand.

cards.simple: New, trendy products. Unpredictable demand, high margin.
cards.example: A limited-edition burger gadget that could flop or sell out.
cards.answer: New products with hard-to-predict demand, short life cycles and higher margins.
traps: Everyday products with steady demand and thin margins.
New products with steady demand and long life cycles.
New products with thin margins and predictable sales.

cards.simple: CHOOSING one supplier when others exist.
cards.example: Bob picks one beef supplier even though there are five around.
cards.answer: Picking just one supplier on purpose, even though others are available.
traps: Using one supplier because nobody else makes the item.
Splitting the order across several suppliers.
Making the item yourself instead of buying it.
cards.confuse: Single = you CHOSE one. Sole = there IS only one.

cards.simple: Only ONE supplier exists, so there's no choice.
cards.hook: Sole = the only one, the sole survivor.
cards.example: A patented grill part that only one company makes.
cards.answer: Using one supplier because it's the only one that offers the item.
traps: Picking one supplier on purpose when others are available.
Using several suppliers to spread out risk.
Using one supplier because it's the cheapest.
cards.confuse: Single = you CHOSE one. Sole = there IS only one.

cards.simple: Buying the same thing from several suppliers.
cards.hook: Don't put all your eggs in one basket.
cards.example: Bob buys beef from two suppliers so one can cover if the other fails.
cards.answer: Buying the same item from more than one supplier so you don't depend on just one.
traps: Buying different items from different suppliers.
Picking one supplier on purpose.
Buying from one supplier that has several warehouses.

cards.simple: Low value, low risk. Strategy: keep it SIMPLE.
cards.hook: Not a big deal either way.
cards.example: Regular napkins, which a dozen suppliers sell.
cards.answer: Cheap items with plenty of suppliers, so keep buying simple.
traps: Cheap items that are hard to get, so protect supply.
Expensive items with plenty of suppliers, so negotiate.
Expensive items that are hard to get, so partner.
cards.confuse: Think of the grid: value (low/high) × risk (low/high).

cards.simple: Low value, high risk. Strategy: PROTECT the supply.
cards.hook: The neck of a bottle is small, but everything gets stuck there.
cards.example: A cheap grill knob that's hard to find. Without it, the grill can't run.
cards.answer: Cheap items that are hard to get, so focus on securing supply.
traps: Cheap items with lots of suppliers, so keep it simple.
Expensive items with lots of suppliers, so negotiate.
Expensive items that are hard to get, so partner.
cards.confuse: Bottleneck = cheap but risky. Strategic = expensive AND risky.

cards.simple: High value, low risk. Strategy: NEGOTIATE hard.
cards.example: Huge flour orders with lots of suppliers competing for them.
cards.answer: Expensive items with plenty of suppliers, so use your buying power to negotiate.
traps: Expensive items that are hard to get, so partner.
Cheap items that are hard to get, so protect supply.
Cheap items with plenty of suppliers, so keep it simple.

cards.simple: High value, high risk. Strategy: PARTNER up.
cards.hook: Strategic = high and high. Kahoot: TRUE.
cards.example: Custom kitchen equipment that only a couple of companies can build.
cards.answer: Expensive items that are hard to get, so build close supplier partnerships.
traps: Expensive items with plenty of suppliers, so negotiate.
Cheap items that are hard to get, so protect supply.
Expensive items that are easy to get, so partner.
cards.confuse: Bottleneck = cheap but risky. Strategic = expensive AND risky.

cards.simple: Do it yourself or pay someone? Look at ALL relevant costs.
cards.hook: Cooking at home vs. ordering DoorDash.
cards.example: Bob compares baking his own buns with buying them from a bakery.
cards.answer: Choosing between producing something yourself or buying it, weighing every relevant cost.
traps: Choosing between producing something yourself or buying it, based only on purchase price.
Choosing which supplier to buy from based on QSDP.
Choosing whether to buy your supplier's company.
cards.confuse: Kahoot: should analyze ALL relevant costs = TRUE.

cards.simple: Doing the work inside the company. The opposite of outsourcing. Protects secrets.
cards.example: Rhode Beauty keeps its blush formula in-house so nobody can copy it.
cards.answer: Keeping work within the company, often to protect know-how.
traps: Hiring an outside company to do the work.
Buying one of your suppliers.
Using several suppliers for the same item.
cards.confuse: Insourcing is about WHO does the work. Backward integration is about BUYING a supplier.

cards.simple: Paying an outside company to do it.
cards.example: A bakery makes Bob's buns.
cards.answer: Paying an outside firm to handle work or supply goods.
traps: Bringing outside work back into the company.
Buying a company that sells to your customers.
Doing all production in-house to protect secrets.

cards.simple: Buying your SUPPLIERS.
cards.hook: Backward = back up the chain, to where stuff comes from.
cards.example: Bob buys the cow farm. Kahoot: a chemical company buys its suppliers.
cards.answer: Taking ownership of the businesses that supply you.
traps: Taking ownership of the businesses that sell to your customers.
Bringing outsourced work back in-house.
Signing long-term contracts with your suppliers.
cards.confuse: Backward = toward suppliers. Forward = toward customers.

cards.simple: Buying toward your CUSTOMERS.
cards.example: A beef farm buys a chain of burger restaurants.
cards.answer: Taking ownership of businesses closer to the end customer, like distributors or stores.
traps: Taking ownership of the businesses that supply you.
Hiring outside firms to sell your product.
Expanding into a brand-new, unrelated industry.
cards.confuse: Backward = toward suppliers. Forward = toward customers.

cards.simple: Protects you if the winning bidder refuses to SIGN.
cards.example: A contractor wins Bob's renovation bid, then ghosts him. The bid bond pays Bob.
cards.answer: Covers the buyer if the winning bidder won't actually sign the contract.
traps: Covers the buyer if the contractor doesn't finish the work to spec.
Covers subcontractors and suppliers if they don't get paid.
Covers the bidder if the buyer cancels the project.
cards.confuse: Bid = SIGN. Performance = COMPLETE. Payment = PAY.

cards.simple: Guarantees the job gets DONE to the agreed specs.
cards.example: The contractor quits halfway. The performance bond covers getting it finished.
cards.answer: Guarantees the contractor completes the work to the agreed requirements.
traps: Guarantees the winning bidder signs the contract.
Guarantees subcontractors and suppliers get paid.
Guarantees the project finishes under budget.
cards.confuse: Bid = SIGN. Performance = COMPLETE. Payment = PAY.

cards.simple: Guarantees workers and suppliers get PAID.
cards.example: The contractor doesn't pay the plumbers. The payment bond pays them.
cards.answer: Protects the subcontractors and suppliers on a job so they get paid.
traps: Protects the buyer if the contractor doesn't finish.
Protects the buyer if the winner won't sign.
Protects the contractor if the buyer pays late.
cards.confuse: Bid = SIGN. Performance = COMPLETE. Payment = PAY.

cards.simple: Several suppliers compete for the job, which keeps costs down.
cards.hook: A bidding war, but in your favor.
cards.example: 4 suppliers bid on Bob's new grill and the price drops.
cards.answer: Having several suppliers compete for a contract to get better prices and terms.
traps: Negotiating one-on-one with a single chosen supplier.
Having suppliers compete, which mostly raises quality but doesn't affect cost.
Asking suppliers for general info about what they can do.
cards.confuse: Kahoot: competitive bidding helps manage costs = TRUE.

cards.simple: Quality, Service, Delivery, Price: how you judge suppliers.
cards.example: Bob rates beef suppliers on meat quality, how they treat him, on-time trucks and price.
cards.answer: Quality, Service, Delivery, Price.
traps: Quantity, Service, Delivery, Price.
Quality, Supply, Demand, Price.
Quality, Service, Distribution, Profit.
cards.question: What do the letters in QSDP stand for?

cards.simple: Make it AFTER the order. NOT much finished inventory.
cards.hook: Like Subway: made when you ask.
cards.example: Bob cooks a custom burger once the customer orders it.
cards.answer: Production starts only after a customer orders, so little finished stock sits around.
traps: Production happens ahead of orders based on forecasts.
Production starts after an order, so lots of finished stock is kept on hand.
Products are made in bulk, then customized at pickup.
cards.confuse: Kahoot: MTO holds large finished-goods inventory = FALSE.

cards.simple: Make it BEFORE orders, then sell it.
cards.hook: Like a vending machine: already made.
cards.example: Pre-packed sandwiches in the grocery store fridge.
cards.answer: Products are made ahead of time from forecasts and held until someone buys.
traps: Products are made only after a customer orders.
Products are made ahead of time only for one customer's contract.
Products ship straight from the supplier to the customer.

cards.simple: Recorded as an ASSET (a current asset).
cards.hook: It's worth money, so it's an asset.
cards.example: Bob's unused beef and buns count as assets.
cards.answer: It's listed as a current asset.
traps: It's listed as a current liability.
It only shows up as an expense on the income statement.
It's listed under owner's equity.
cards.question: How is inventory recorded on the balance sheet?

cards.simple: Every dollar saved on purchasing goes straight to profit.
cards.hook: Save a buck, make a buck.
cards.example: Bob saves $5,000 on ingredients, so profit goes up $5,000.
cards.answer: Savings on purchasing drop straight to the bottom line, all else equal.
traps: Raising sales always helps profit more than cutting purchase costs.
Spending more on purchasing leads to higher profit.
Purchasing savings mostly get eaten by higher holding costs.

questions.question: Bob uses 25 lb of beef a day, delivery takes 4 days, and he keeps 20 lb of safety stock. When should he reorder?

questions.why: A requisition is the internal request; the PO goes to the supplier.

questions.question: At what point does a purchase order become legally binding?
choices: When it's emailed to the supplier
When the supplier accepts its terms
questions.answer: When the supplier accepts its terms

questions.question: Chipotle already knows exactly what avocados it needs and just wants each supplier's price per case. Which document should it send?
questions.why: RFQ = detailed price quotes for specified items.

questions.question: A shipment of sneakers is on a container ship heading to Nike's warehouse. What kind of inventory is it?
A bakery's supply of oven cleaner and spare mixer parts is which kind of inventory?
questions.why: MRO keeps things running and never ends up in the product.

questions.question: Apple buys a custom chip that is very expensive and that only one or two factories in the world can make. Which category is it?
questions.why: High value + high risk = strategic, so partner closely.

questions.question: A contractor wins the bid for a new stadium but then refuses to sign the contract. Which bond protects the buyer?
questions.why: Bid = sign. Performance = complete. Payment = pay.
